title: OPPOSITION: Arkada's Mini MBrace (003195484)
text:
OPPOSITION Nо B 3 195 484

Orifarm Generics A/S, Energivej 15, Postboks 69, Lindved, 5260 Odense S, Denmark (opponent), represented by Bugge Valentin Advokatpartnerselskab, Havnegade 25, 1058 København K, Denmark (professional representative) 

a g a i n s t

Adrian Arkada Instytut Podologii, Walońska 9/2u, 50413 Wrocław, Poland (applicant).

On 30/07/2026, the Opposition Division takes the following

DECISION:

REASONS

On 08/05/2023, the opponent filed an opposition against all the goods and services of European Union trade mark application No 18 816 656 ‘Arkada's Mini MBrace’ (word mark). The opposition is based on, inter alia, international trade mark registration designating the European Union No 1 661 895 ‘MBRACE’ (word mark). The opponent invoked Article 8(1)(b) EUTMR.

LIKELIHOOD OF CONFUSION — ARTICLE 8(1)(b) EUTMR

Pursuant to Article 8(1)(b) EUTMR, a likelihood of confusion exists if there is a risk that the public might believe that the goods or services in question, under the assumption that they bear the marks in question, come from the same undertaking or, as the case may be, from economically linked undertakings. Whether a likelihood of confusion exists depends on the appreciation in a global assessment of several factors, which are interdependent. These factors include the similarity of the signs, the similarity of the goods and services, the distinctiveness of the earlier mark, the distinctive and dominant elements of the conflicting signs, and the relevant public.

The opposition is based on more than one earlier trade mark. The Opposition Division finds it appropriate to first examine the opposition in relation to the opponent’s international trade mark registration designating the European Union No 1 661 895.

a) The goods and services

The goods and services on which the opposition is based are the following:

Class 3: 	Cosmetics, including cosmetic preparations for skin care, moisturizing preparations, moisturizing creams, non-medicated cosmetic preparations.

Class 5: 	Pharmaceuticals; sanitary preparations for medical purposes; dietetic foods and preparations adapted for medical use; dietary supplements for humans; vitamins and vitamin preparations.

Class 35: 	Retail and wholesale of cosmetics, including cosmetic preparations for skin care, moisturizing preparations, moisturizing creams and non-medicinal cosmetic preparations, pharmaceutical preparations, sanitary preparations for medical purposes, dietetic foods and preparations adapted for medical use, dietary supplements for humans, vitamins and vitamin preparations.

The contested goods and services are the following:

Class 3: 	Cosmetics and cosmetic preparations; cosmetic preparations for skin care; body cleaning and beauty care preparations; skin, eye and nail care preparations; toiletries; moisturising creams, lotions and gels; cosmetic soaps; beauty milk; beauty masks; beauty serums; ointments for cosmetic use; beauty lotions; perfumery and fragrances; body splash; skin cleansers; cleansing lotions; essential oils and aromatic extracts; lotions for cosmetic purposes; face oils; shampoos; hair nourishers; exfoliants for the cleansing of the skin; cosmetic body scrubs; bath preparations; non-medicated bath salts; pedicure preparations; nail cosmetics; nail cream; nail varnish; preparations for reinforcing the nails; nail repair preparations; dressings for nail reconstruction; cuticle softeners; moist wipes for sanitary and cosmetic purposes; fingernail tips; degreasing sprays.

Class 5: 	Food supplements; pharmaceuticals and natural remedies; medicinal ointments; tissue-regenerative pharmaceutical preparations; antiviral disinfectants; nail sanitizing preparations; hand-sanitizing preparations; preparations for callouses; salts for medical purposes; nail care preparations for medical use; anti-fungal dermatological preparations for use on the nails; styptic preparations; medical dressings, coverings and applicators; adhesive tapes for medical purposes.

Class 8: 	Manicure and pedicure tools; pedicure sets; manicure sets; nail nippers; nail scissors; emery files; foot file roller heads for removing hardened skin; tweezers; rasps [hand tools]; cases for manicure instruments; nail buffers for use in manicure; podiatry hand tools; hand tools for shaping toenail clamps; hand tools for shaping clamps of metal.

Class 41: 	Education and instruction services; provision of training courses; vocational training services; educational seminars relating to beauty therapy; educational services relating to beauty therapy; instruction in cosmetic beauty; educational services in the nature of beauty schools; training, in relation to the following fields: the use of manicure and pedicure apparatus and instruments.

Class 44: 	Skin care salons; beauty salon services; nail salon services; manicure and pedicure services; cosmetic treatment; podiatrist.

An interpretation of the wording of the goods or services is required to determine the scope of protection of these goods or services.

In this respect, the General Court has confirmed that the use of the term ‘in particular’ indicates that the specific goods or services are only examples of items included in the preceding category and that protection is not restricted to them (09/04/2003, T‑224/01, NU-TRIDE / TUFFTRIDE, EU:T:2003:107, § 41). The same considerations must be found to apply to other synonymous terms like ꞌespeciallyꞌ, ‘for example’, ‘such as’ or ‘including’ (in the list of opponent´s goods and services in Classes 3 and 35). In other words, the use of any such terms in the specifications of goods or services only introduces non-exhaustive lists of examples.

As a preliminary remark, it is to be noted that according to Article 33(7) EUTMR, goods or services are not regarded as being similar to or dissimilar from each other on the ground that they appear in the same or different classes under the Nice Classification.

The relevant factors relating to the comparison of the goods or services include, inter alia, their nature, their intended purpose, their method of use and whether they are in competition with each other or are complementary (‘the Canon criteria’). It is also necessary to take into account, besides the Canon criteria, other factors, namely distribution channels, the relevant public and the usual origin of the goods or services (02/06/2021, T‑177/20, Hispano Suiza / Hispano Suiza, EU:T:2021:312, § 21-22).

Contested goods in Class 3

The contested cosmetics and cosmetic preparations; cosmetic preparations for skin care; body cleaning and beauty care preparations; skin, eye and nail care preparations; toiletries; moisturising creams, lotions and gels; cosmetic soaps; beauty milk; beauty masks; beauty serums; ointments for cosmetic use; beauty lotions; body splash; skin cleansers; cleansing lotions; lotions for cosmetic purposes; face oils; shampoos; hair nourishers; exfoliants for the cleansing of the skin; cosmetic body scrubs; bath preparations; non-medicated bath salts; pedicure preparations; nail cosmetics; nail cream; nail varnish; preparations for reinforcing the nails; nail repair preparations; dressings for nail reconstruction; cuticle softeners; moist wipes for sanitary and cosmetic purposes are identical to the opponent’s cosmetics because the opponent’s goods either include, as a broader category, or overlap with, the contested goods.

The contested fingernail tips are highly similar to the opponent´s cosmetics as they have the same purpose. They usually coincide in producer, relevant public and distribution channels. Furthermore, they are complementary.

The contested perfumery and fragrances; essential oils and aromatic extracts are similar to the opponent's cosmetics. Cosmetics include preparations for enhancing or protecting the appearance, condition or fragrance of the body, while perfumery and fragrances are used to impart a pleasant scent and essential oils and aromatic extracts for cosmetic purposes are fragrant compounds that may be used in the care of the skin or as ingredients in cosmetic products. Accordingly, these goods may have complementary or overlapping purposes. They can coincide in their relevant public, distribution channels and usual producers.

The contested degreasing sprays are dissimilar to all the opponent’s goods and services in Classes 3, 5 and 35. The contested goods are cleaning preparations, other than for personal use intended for removing grease and cleaning surfaces, whereas the opponent’s goods are intended for personal care, skin treatment, medical treatment and maintaining or improving human health. Their purpose and method of use differ. They have different functions, target different consumer needs and are not interchangeable. In addition, the contested goods are dissimilar to the opponent´s services in Class 35. The contested goods are tangible products intended for cleaning and degreasing purposes, whereas the opponent’s services consist of the commercialisation of goods through retail and wholesale activities. They have different natures, purposes and methods of use. The mere fact that retail and wholesale services may concern certain goods is not sufficient, in itself, to establish similarity between the services and the goods concerned. For similarity to exist, there must be specific characteristics in common, such as the fact that the goods and services have the same purpose, are complementary or are usually provided by the same undertakings. In the present case, degreasing sprays are not the type of goods that are normally associated with the retail and wholesale of cosmetics, pharmaceutical preparations or healthcare products covered by the opponent’s services. Moreover, the contested goods and the opponent’s services are directed at different commercial functions and originate from different providers.

Therefore, the contested degreasing sprays are dissimilar to all the opponent’s goods and services in Classes 3, 5 and 35.

Contested goods in Class 5

The contested food supplements are included in the broad category of the opponent’s dietary supplements for humans. Therefore, they are identical.

The contested pharmaceuticals and natural remedies; medicinal ointments; tissue-regenerative pharmaceutical preparations; preparations for callouses; salts for medical purposes; nail care preparations for medical use; anti-fungal dermatological preparations for use on the nails; styptic preparations are identical to the opponent’s pharmaceuticals either because they are identically contained in both lists (including synonyms) or because the opponent’s goods include, are included in, or overlap with, the contested goods.

The contested antiviral disinfectants; nail sanitizing preparations; hand-sanitizing preparations are included in the broader category of the opponent's sanitary preparations for medical purposes. Therefore, they are identical.

The contested medical dressings, coverings and applicators; adhesive tapes for medical purposes are similar to the opponent’s sanitary preparations for medical purposes. While the contested medical dressings and coverings are used to protect a wound, promote healing and prevent infection, the contested applicators are used to apply medications, ointments or other substances to a specific area of the body, and the contested adhesive tapes for medical purposes are used to secure dressings, bandages or medical devices and to assist in wound care and treatment. All these goods coincide in their distribution channels (i.e. those for medical supplies), in their relevant public (e.g. hospitals), and in their usual producers.

Contested goods in Class 8

The contested manicure and pedicure tools; pedicure sets; manicure sets; nail nippers; nail scissors; emery files; foot file roller heads for removing hardened skin; tweezers; rasps [hand tools]; cases for manicure instruments; nail buffers for use in manicure are similar to a low degree to the opponent's cosmetics because they coincide in purpose and they usually coincide in relevant public and distribution channels.

The contested hand tools for shaping toenail clamps; hand tools for shaping clamps of metal; podiatry hand tools differ from all the opponent´s goods and services in Classes 3, 5 and 35 in their nature, purpose and method of use. The contested goods are specialised hand-operated podiatry instruments/tools intended for shaping metal clamps used in toenail correction treatments and for carrying out podiatric procedures. They are designed for shaping toenail correction clamps rather than forming part of a pedicure set for routine nail care. The conflicting goods and services are normally provided by different commercial undertakings, distributed through different trade channels and directed, mainly, at different consumers. Although some of them may be used in the healthcare field or may be encountered by the same professional users, this circumstance alone is insufficient to establish similarity. Furthermore, the contested goods are neither in competition nor complementary with the opponent's goods or services. Therefore, these contested goods are dissimilar to the opponent's goods and services in Classes 3, 5 and 35.

Contested services in Class 41

The contested education and instruction services; provision of training courses; vocational training services; educational seminars relating to beauty therapy; educational services relating to beauty therapy; instruction in cosmetic beauty; educational services in the nature of beauty schools; training, in relation to the following fields: the use of manicure and pedicure apparatus and instruments differ from all the opponent´s goods and services in Classes 3, 5 and 35 in their nature, purpose and method of use.

The contested services consist of the provision of knowledge, instruction and professional training, particularly in the field of beauty therapy, cosmetic beauty and the use of manicure and pedicure instruments. 

The goods and services at issue have different functions. The purpose of the contested services is to educate and train individuals by providing theoretical and practical skills, whereas the opponent’s goods are intended to be consumed or used for cosmetic, medical or health purposes. The opponent´s services in Class 35 have the purpose of selling or distributing goods and do not involve the provision of education or professional training.

Although the contested training services relate to beauty therapy, cosmetics and the use of manicure and pedicure apparatus and instruments, this connection is not sufficient to establish similarity with cosmetic products or healthcare preparations. The relevant public may encounter these goods and services in the same broad commercial sector, namely beauty and personal care, but they are not interchangeable, do not serve the same purpose and are not in competition.

Furthermore, the providers of the respective goods and services are generally different. Beauty schools and training providers are not normally the same undertakings as manufacturers of cosmetics, pharmaceutical companies or wholesalers and retailers of healthcare products. While some beauty establishments may offer training courses and sell cosmetic products as complementary activities, this does not establish a sufficiently close relationship between the goods and services concerned.

Consequently, the contested services in Class 41 are dissimilar to the opponent’s goods and services in Classes 3, 5 and 35.

Contested services in Class 44

The contested skin care salons; beauty salon services; nail salon services; manicure and pedicure services; cosmetic treatment are similar to the opponent’s cosmetics in Class 3, since they have the same overall purpose (beauty care), their distribution channels can overlap and their target public is the same. Furthermore, they are complementary, as it can be necessary to use the contested services to perform the opponent’s goods and vice versa.

The conflicting services can be offered by the same undertakings carrying out commercial activities in the field of beauty and skincare. They have the same overall purpose: beauty and skincare, their distribution channels can overlap and the target public is the same (26/05/2015, R 1443/2014-4, KOKO NAIL / KIKO et al., § 23). This is because beauty salons and similar establishments frequently offer cosmetic and beauty products for sale, either for immediate use during treatments or for customers' subsequent use at home. The sale of cosmetic products is not merely ancillary to the provision of beauty services but may also constitute an independent commercial activity. Consumers may choose to purchase cosmetics in these specialised establishments because they perceive the products as professionally recommended or more reliable. 

The contested podiatrist is different to all the opponent’s goods and services in Classes 3, 5 and 35. Podiatry services are medical services aimed at diagnosing, preventing and treating disorders and diseases affecting the feet and lower limbs. The contested services and the opponent’s goods and services differ in their nature, purpose and method of use. Furthermore, they are normally provided by different undertakings through different distribution channels. Although podiatrists may, in the course of providing treatment, recommend or supply certain medical or cosmetic products, this does not alter the fundamentally different nature of the respective goods and services, nor does it create a sufficiently close connection for them to be regarded as complementary. Consequently, they are dissimilar.

b) Relevant public — degree of attention

The average consumer of the category of products concerned is deemed to be reasonably well informed and reasonably observant and circumspect. It should also be borne in mind that the average consumer’s degree of attention is likely to vary according to the category of goods or services in question (22/06/1999, C-342/97, Lloyd Schuhfabrik, EU:C:1999:323, § 26).

In the present case, the goods and services found to be identical or similar to varying degrees target the public at large and business customers with specific professional knowledge or expertise.

The degree of attention may vary from average to high, depending on the price, the specialised nature, the terms and conditions of the goods and services purchased, or on whether they have an impact on consumers’ health.

In this regard it is noted that it is apparent from the case-law that, insofar as pharmaceutical preparations, whether or not issued on prescription, are concerned, the relevant public’s degree of attention is relatively high (15/12/2010, T‑331/09, TOLPOSAN / TONOPAN, EU:T:2010:520, § 26; 15/03/2012, T‑288/08, ZYDUS / ZIMBUS, EU:T:2012:124, § 36). In particular, medical professionals have a high degree of attentiveness when prescribing medicines. Non-professionals also have a higher degree of attention, regardless of whether the pharmaceuticals are sold without prescription, as these goods affect their state of health. This also applies to all the relevant goods in Class 5 as they all have an impact on consumers’ health. 

c) The signs

The relevant territory is the European Union.

The global appreciation of the visual, aural or conceptual similarity of the marks in question must be based on the overall impression given by the marks, bearing in mind, in particular, their distinctive and dominant components (11/11/1997, C-251/95, Sabèl, EU:C:1997:528, § 23).

The unitary character of the European Union trade mark means that an earlier European Union trade mark can be relied on in opposition proceedings against any application for registration of a European Union trade mark that would adversely affect the protection of the first mark, even if only in relation to the perception of consumers in part of the European Union (18/09/2008, C-514/06 P, Armafoam, EU:C:2008:511, § 57). This applies by analogy to international registrations designating the European Union. Therefore, a likelihood of confusion for only part of the relevant public of the European Union is sufficient to reject the contested application.

The contested sign´s verbal element ‘Arkada´s’ will be perceived by at least part of the relevant public, in particular Polish-, Czech- and Slovak-speaking consumers, as a distinctive meaning ‘arcade’ that could lead to a conceptual difference between the signs and potentially have an impact on the outcome of the opposition. However, both signs' verbal elements ‘Arkada´s’ and ‘MBRACE’ are meaningless in certain territories, for example in France, where they will, therefore, be perceived as fanciful terms. 

Therefore, the Opposition Division finds it appropriate to focus the comparison of the signs on the French-speaking part of the public for whom ‘Arkada´s’ and ‘MBRACE’ are meaningless terms and therefore distinctive. 

Although the additional verbal element ‘Mini’ of the contested sign is, inter alia, used as an adjective to indicate ‘smallness’, ‘brevity’ by the French-speaking public (information extracted from Larousse dictionary online on 27/07/2026 at https://www.larousse.fr/dictionnaires/francais/mini/51595), insofar as it could be allusive to the characteristics of the goods or could refer to the extent of the services offered, it is, at best, weak and, therefore, does not affect the perception of the distinctive verbal elements. 

Visually and aurally, the signs coincide in the element 'MBRACE'/'MBrace' and its pronunciation. They differ in the additional contested sign’s verbal elements 'Arkada's Mini' and their pronunciation. Despite this difference between the signs, the identical verbal element 'MBRACE' constitutes the entirety of the earlier mark, and its presence in the contested sign indicates a similarity between the signs (21/02/2024, T-175/23, LifeAfter / life, § 74; 28/10/2009, T-273/08, First-On-Skin / FIRST, §31). Further, the consideration that the consumer normally attaches more importance to the initial part of a mark cannot apply in all cases and call into question the principle that the examination of the similarity of signs must be based on the overall impression produced by them. There is no reason to believe that average consumers, who are reasonably well informed, observant and circumspect, will systematically disregard the subsequent part of the verbal element of a trade mark to the extent that they only remember the first part (07/06/2023, T-33/22, Porto insígnia / Insignia et al., EU:T:2023:316, § 56-57). Therefore, the differing additional verbal elements ‘Arkada's’ and ‘Mini’ at the beginning of the contested sign are not capable of detracting the consumer´s attention from perceiving both signs as also consisting of or containing the term ‘MBRACE’, and the signs are, therefore, visually and aurally similar to a below-average degree. 

Conceptually, reference is made to the previous assertions concerning the semantic content conveyed by the marks. Whereas the earlier mark is meaningless, the relevant public assessed will perceive a concept of ‘Mini’ in the contested sign. To that extent, the marks are conceptually not similar. However, this conceptual difference is of very limited relevance in the overall comparison of signs, as it stems from an, at best, weak meaning.

As the signs have been found similar in at least one aspect of the comparison, the examination of likelihood of confusion will proceed.

d) Distinctiveness of the earlier mark

The distinctiveness of the earlier mark is one of the factors to be taken into account in the global assessment of likelihood of confusion.

The opponent did not explicitly claim that its mark is particularly distinctive by virtue of intensive use or reputation.

Consequently, the assessment of the distinctiveness of the earlier mark will rest on its distinctiveness per se. In the present case, the earlier trade mark has no meaning for any of the goods in question from the perspective of the public under assessment. Therefore, the distinctiveness of the earlier mark must be seen as normal.

e) Global assessment, other arguments and conclusion

The appreciation of likelihood of confusion on the part of the public depends, inter alia, on the recognition of the earlier mark on the market, the association that can be made with the registered mark, and the degree of similarity between the marks and between the goods or services identified. It must be appreciated globally, taking into account all factors relevant to the circumstances of the case (22/06/1999, C-342/97, Lloyd Schuhfabrik, EU:C:1999:323, § 18; 11/11/1997, C-251/95, Sabèl, EU:C:1997:528, § 22).

Evaluating likelihood of confusion implies some interdependence between the relevant factors and, in particular, a similarity between the marks and between the goods or services. Therefore, a lesser degree of similarity between goods and services may be offset by a greater degree of similarity between the marks and vice versa (29/09/1998, C-39/97, Canon, EU:C:1998:442, § 17).

The goods and services are partly identical, partly similar to varying degrees, and partly dissimilar. The relevant public is the public at large and business customers with specific professional knowledge or expertise, whose degree of attention may vary from average to high. The earlier mark has a normal degree of distinctiveness. The signs are visually and aurally similar to a below-average degree in that they share the verbal element 'MBRACE', which is the only verbal element of the earlier mark. The signs are conceptually not similar. However, this conceptual difference is of limited relevance in the overall comparison of signs, as it stems from a, at best, weak meaning of the verbal element ‘Mini’. The difference in the contested sign’s additional verbal elements 'Arkada's' and 'Mini' are not enough to counteract the similarities. As a rule, when the earlier trade mark is wholly incorporated in the contested sign and performs an independent and distinctive role therein, this is an indication that the two signs are similar (13/06/2012, T 519/10, SG Seikoh Giken, EU:T:2012:291, § 27; 24/01/2012, T 260/08, Visual Map, EU:T:2012:23, § 32; 22/05/2012, T 179/11, Seven Summits, EU:T:2012:254, § 26).

Likelihood of confusion covers situations where the consumer directly confuses the trade marks themselves, or where the consumer makes a connection between the conflicting signs and assumes that the goods/services covered are from the same or economically linked undertakings (29/09/1998, C‑39/97, Canon, EU:C:1998:442, § 29). In the present case, it is highly conceivable that the relevant consumer will perceive the contested mark as a sub-brand, a variation of the earlier mark, configured in a different way according to the type of goods that it designates (23/10/2002, T‑104/01, Fifties / Miss Fifties (fig.), EU:T:2002:262, § 49). 

Considering all the above, the Opposition Division finds that there is a likelihood of confusion on the part of the French-speaking part of the public and, therefore, the opposition is partly well founded on the basis of the opponent’s international trade mark registration designating the European Union No 1 661 895. It should be recalled that, as stated above in section c) of this decision, a likelihood of confusion for only part of the relevant public of the European Union is sufficient to reject the contested application.

It follows from the above that the contested trade mark must be rejected for the goods and services found to be identical or similar to varying degrees to those of the earlier trade mark, including the ones similar to a low degree only taking into account the similarities between the signs and the interdependence principle mentioned above.

The rest of the contested goods and services are dissimilar. As the identity or similarity of goods and services is a necessary condition for the application of Article 8(1)(b) EUTMR, the opposition based on this Article and directed at these goods and services cannot be successful.

The opponent has also based its opposition on the following earlier trade marks:

1)	European Union trade mark registration No 18 750 965, (figurative mark) for goods in Classes 3 and 5;

      2)	Danish trade mark registration No 2022 00568, ‘MBRACE’ (word mark) for the same goods and services in Classes 3, 5 and 35 as those covered by international trade mark registration designating the European Union No 1 661 895, already compared above.

Since these marks cover the same or a narrower scope of goods and services, the outcome cannot be different with respect to goods and services for which the opposition has already been rejected; no likelihood of confusion exists with respect to those goods and services.

COSTS

According to Article 109(1) EUTMR, the losing party in opposition proceedings must bear the fees and costs incurred by the other party. According to Article 109(3) EUTMR, where each party succeeds on some heads and fails on others, or if reasons of equity so dictate, the Opposition Division will decide a different apportionment of costs.

Since the opposition is successful for only some of the contested goods and services, both parties have succeeded on some heads and failed on others. Consequently, each party has to bear its own costs.

The Opposition Division

According to Article 67 EUTMR, any party adversely affected by this decision has a right to appeal against this decision. According to Article 68 EUTMR, notice of appeal must be filed in writing at the Office within two months of the date of notification of this decision. It must be filed in the language of the proceedings in which the decision subject to appeal was taken. Furthermore, a written statement of the grounds for appeal must be filed within four months of the same date. The notice of appeal will be deemed to have been filed only when the appeal fee of EUR 720 has been paid.
